ERR-SYN-01.assumed: You probably expected SQL to accept the clauses in any order, to read past a small typo in a keyword, or to read a name with a space in it, such as `AS my column`, as one name.
ERR-SYN-01.why: SQL recognises keywords only by their exact spelling, and the clauses must come in a fixed written order. A name ends at the first space unless it is in double quotes, so the word after the space looks like a keyword in the wrong place. The engine stops at the first word it does not expect, and its message names that word.
ERR-SYN-01.model: Write the clauses in this order: SELECT, FROM (with any JOIN), WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Then check the spelling of the keywords near the word the message names. A column name you give with AS needs no space: write `AS my_column`, or put the name in double quotes, as in `AS "my column"`.

ERR-SYN-02.assumed: You probably expected the engine to recognise a name that is close to the real one: a column, a table or a function.
ERR-SYN-02.why: SQL only finds names spelled exactly as they exist: a column in one of the tables your query reads, a table in the schema, or a function the engine knows. Capital letters do not matter here, but a typo, a singular instead of a plural, or a column from a table that is not in your FROM clause all count as unknown.
ERR-SYN-02.model: Copy table and column names exactly from the schema panel, check that each column belongs to a table in your FROM clause, and check the spelling of each function name, such as COUNT or ROUND.

ERR-SYN-03.assumed: You probably expected the engine to work out which table `{column}` should come from.
ERR-SYN-03.why: `{column}` exists in more than one of the tables in your query, and SQL will not guess which one you mean.
ERR-SYN-03.model: Write the table's alias in front of the column everywhere you use it, as in `alias.{column}`, where alias is the short name you gave that table in FROM or JOIN.

ERR-SYN-04.assumed: You probably expected the engine to see where each piece of text, bracket or list ends, even with a quote, bracket or comma missing or extra.
ERR-SYN-04.why: SQL uses quotes, brackets and commas to mark where each part of the query starts and stops. One unclosed quote or bracket swallows everything after it, so the engine reaches the end of the query still waiting for it to close.
ERR-SYN-04.model: Check that every opening quote and bracket has its closing partner, and that a comma separates every two items in a list.

ERR-SYN-05.assumed: You probably expected WHERE to filter on a total, a count or an average.
ERR-SYN-05.why: SQL runs WHERE on single rows, before GROUP BY builds any groups or totals, so an aggregate such as `SUM(...)` or `COUNT(*)` cannot be used there.
ERR-SYN-05.model: Keep conditions on single rows in WHERE, and put conditions on totals in HAVING, after GROUP BY, for example `HAVING COUNT(*) > 10`.

ERR-SYN-06.assumed: You probably expected a name you gave a total or a count in SELECT (with AS) to be usable in WHERE.
ERR-SYN-06.why: WHERE filters single rows before any totals are worked out, and before SELECT names its columns. So it cannot test an aggregate such as `COUNT(*)` or `SUM(...)`, not even through its alias.
ERR-SYN-06.model: Test a total in HAVING, after GROUP BY, and repeat the aggregate there: `GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` instead of `WHERE n_products > 1`. Or work the total out in a subquery and filter it with WHERE in the outer query.

ERR-SYN-07.assumed: You probably meant "{column}" as a piece of text, which is what double quotes mean in many other languages.
ERR-SYN-07.why: In SQL, double quotes mark the name of a column or table, and only single quotes mark text, so the engine looked for a column called {column} and found none.
ERR-SYN-07.model: Put text in single quotes, as in `'{column}'`, and compare values with `=` and `<>`, the standard SQL operators.

ERR-SYN-08.assumed: You probably expected WHERE to filter on the result of a window function, such as a rank, a row number or a running total.
ERR-SYN-08.why: SQL works out window functions after WHERE has already picked the rows, so WHERE cannot test `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)` or any other window function.
ERR-SYN-08.model: Work the window function out in a CTE or subquery, give it a name, and filter that name with WHERE in the outer query: `WITH ranked AS (SELECT product_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY units DESC) AS rn FROM t) SELECT product_id FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3`.

ERR-SEM-01.assumed: You probably expected SQL to show a column next to your totals without being told how to combine its values in each group.
ERR-SEM-01.why: After GROUP BY, each group becomes one row. A column that is neither in GROUP BY nor inside an aggregate can hold many different values within one group, and SQL will not pick one for you.
ERR-SEM-01.model: Add the column to GROUP BY if the question wants one row per that column too (this changes the grain), or wrap it in an aggregate such as `MAX(...)` if one value per group is enough. If the column is only read by a CASE label, group by the label instead (its name, its position or the whole CASE). If it sits in a HAVING test on single rows, move that test to WHERE.

ERR-SEM-02.assumed: You probably expected AND to keep the rows that have either value, as in `country_code = 'NL' AND country_code = 'BE'`.
ERR-SEM-02.why: AND keeps a row only when both conditions are true for that same row, and a column holds one value in each row. A condition that asks one column to equal two different values at once can never be true, so the query returns no rows at all.
ERR-SEM-02.model: To keep the rows with either value, use OR or IN: `WHERE country_code IN ('NL', 'BE')`. Keep AND for conditions on different columns, such as `country_code = 'NL' AND store_type = 'outlet'`.

ERR-SEM-03.assumed: You probably expected the tables to pair up on their shared ID by themselves.
ERR-SEM-03.why: Without a condition that links a key in one table to the same key in the other, SQL pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second. That gives far more rows than either table has, and every total comes out much too big.
ERR-SEM-03.model: Give every JOIN an ON condition that matches the link the schema panel shows, as in `FROM order_lines ol JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = ol.order_id`. Then check the row count: an inner join along a 1:N link never returns more rows than the N side has.

ERR-SEM-04.assumed: You probably expected `= NULL` to find the missing values.
ERR-SEM-04.why: In SQL, a comparison with NULL is unknown, not true, so `= NULL` and `<> NULL` keep no rows.
ERR-SEM-04.model: Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL` to test for missing values.

ERR-SEM-05.assumed: You probably expected a subquery used as one value to give back one value, however many rows match it.
ERR-SEM-05.why: A subquery used as a single value, in the SELECT list or after `=`, `<` or `>`, must return at most one row each time it is worked out. Yours returned more than one for at least one row, and SQL will not pick one of them for you. A filter or a link that looks unique can still match two rows on some data, such as two products tied at a category's top price or a product with two price versions, so the same query can work on one dataset and fail on another.
ERR-SEM-05.model: Make the subquery return one value whatever the data holds: wrap the column in an aggregate, as in `(SELECT MAX(ph.list_price_eur) FROM price_history ph WHERE ph.product_id = p.product_id)`, or link it to the outer row on a column that is unique in the inner table. When any of several values will do, compare with `IN (...)` or `EXISTS (...)` instead of `=`.

ERR-LOG-00.assumed: You probably expected this query to answer the question as it is written.
ERR-LOG-00.why: The app could not match this answer to one common mistake, so the details shown with it, either the rows that differ from the expected result or the engine's message, are the best clue.
ERR-LOG-00.model: Check each clause against the question in the order SQL runs them: the table (FROM), the rows to keep (WHERE), one row per what (GROUP BY), the group filter (HAVING), the columns and numbers (SELECT), then the order and cut-off (ORDER BY, LIMIT). If you have a result, compare one missing row with one extra row to see which clause is off.

ERR-LOG-01.assumed: You probably expected a join to keep each row of the first table once.
ERR-LOG-01.why: A join repeats a row once for every matching row on the other side. An order with three lines appears three times after a join to `order_lines`, so a value stored once per order and summed after the join is counted three times. A product in two promotions, or with several price versions or competitor prices, repeats in the same way.
ERR-LOG-01.model: Check the grain of both tables in the schema panel before you join. Add up the "many" side first, to one row per key, in a CTE, then join that result: `WITH line_totals AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id)`. Compare the row counts before and after the join.

ERR-LOG-02.assumed: You probably expected WHERE and HAVING to do the same job, so the condition went into the wrong one.
ERR-LOG-02.why: WHERE removes single rows before they are grouped, and HAVING removes whole groups after their totals are computed. A condition in the wrong place filters different rows, so the groups or their totals change.
ERR-LOG-02.model: Ask of each condition whether it is about one row or about a group's total. Conditions on rows, such as `country_code = 'BE'`, go in WHERE before GROUP BY; conditions on totals, such as `COUNT(*) > 10`, go in HAVING after it.

ERR-LOG-03.assumed: You probably expected every row to be kept or to get a label, but `<>`, `NOT IN` and `NOT LIKE` drop rows with a missing value, and a CASE with no ELSE leaves every row no WHEN matched as NULL.
ERR-LOG-03.why: A comparison with NULL is unknown, not true, so a filter such as `country_code <> 'NL'` drops the rows with no country_code along with the NL rows. In the same way, a CASE with no ELSE returns NULL for every row that no WHEN branch matches.
ERR-LOG-03.model: When the question counts rows with a missing value, keep them explicitly, for example `WHERE country_code <> 'NL' OR country_code IS NULL`. When every row needs a label, end the CASE with an ELSE.

ERR-LOG-04.assumed: You probably expected every form of COUNT to give the same number.
ERR-LOG-04.why: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(col)` counts only the rows where col is not NULL, and `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts each different value once. When the data has NULLs or repeated values, the three give different answers.
ERR-LOG-04.model: Match the count to the question's words: 'how many rows' is `COUNT(*)`, 'how many have a value' is `COUNT(col)`, and 'how many different' or 'how many unique' is `COUNT(DISTINCT col)`.

ERR-LOG-05.assumed: You probably expected dividing one whole number by another, or a CAST to INTEGER, to keep the decimals.
ERR-LOG-05.why: In PostgreSQL and SQL Server, and with `//` in DuckDB, a whole number divided by a whole number drops everything after the decimal point, so 3 / 4 gives 0 and rates come out as whole numbers. DuckDB's `/` keeps the decimals, but online SQL tests often run on engines that do not. A CAST to INTEGER also gives a whole number: DuckDB rounds it, so `CAST(8.7 AS INTEGER)` is 9.
ERR-LOG-05.model: Make one side a decimal before you divide, for example `clicks * 1.0 / views`. This works the same way on every engine. To round, wrap the final result in `ROUND(x, n)` instead of casting it to INTEGER.

ERR-LOG-06.assumed: You probably expected your range to keep exactly the days the question names, from its first day to its last day, whatever the column holds.
ERR-LOG-06.why: This is about the day at each edge of the range. The question names a first and a last day, and every one of them must be in. On a DATE column, `> '2025-03-01'` leaves out 1 March, `< '2025-03-31'` leaves out 31 March, and starting on 28 February or ending on 1 April adds a day; ending on the first day of the last month or year leaves out the rest of it. On a timestamp, a date means midnight at the start of that day, so `= '2025-03-31'` finds only midnight and `BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'` misses everything later on 31 March. Period boundaries work the same way: a band for a month, quarter or half-year that ends with `<` its last day puts that day in the next period, and a filter on a week or month column keeps or drops whole weeks or months at the edges. A word such as 'over' or 'at least' that you read the wrong way, or a BETWEEN with its ends reversed, is a different mistake: read the wording for each end.
ERR-LOG-06.model: Use a half-open range: on or after the first day, and before the day after the last one, as in `col >= '2025-03-01' AND col < '2025-04-01'` for all of March. It works the same on a DATE and on a timestamp. Filter on the date itself, not on a week or month column, unless the question asks for whole weeks or months. Then check the rows on the first and the last day.

ERR-LOG-07.assumed: You probably expected your GROUP BY to give one row per thing the question asks about.
ERR-LOG-07.why: GROUP BY makes one row for each different combination of the columns you list. An extra column splits each group into smaller ones, and a missing column or a missing GROUP BY merges them, so your rows no longer match the 'per' in the question. A scalar subquery has the same trap: one that is not tied to the row's group works on a different grain, so it repeats the same number on every row.
ERR-LOG-07.model: Find the 'for each' or 'per' phrase in the question and group by exactly those columns. Then select those same columns plus the numbers the question asks for, and nothing else. For a subquery in the SELECT or the WHERE, tie it to the same group with `WHERE inner_table.col = outer_table.col`, so it answers for that row's group only.

ERR-LOG-08.assumed: You probably expected each value to appear only once in your list.
ERR-LOG-08.why: SELECT returns one row for every row it reads, so a value shared by several rows, such as a brand with many products, appears once for each of them.
ERR-LOG-08.model: When the question asks for a list of different values, such as 'which brands' or 'each country once', add DISTINCT: `SELECT DISTINCT brand FROM products`.

ERR-LOG-09.assumed: You probably expected DISTINCT to remove only true copies of the same record.
ERR-LOG-09.why: DISTINCT keeps one row from each set of identical rows, and inside an aggregate it keeps one of each value, even when those rows are different records. Two products with the same cost are still two products, but `SUM(DISTINCT unit_cost_eur)` counts that cost only once.
ERR-LOG-09.model: Remove DISTINCT unless the question asks for different values. To count unique things, apply DISTINCT to their ID, as in `COUNT(DISTINCT product_id)`.

ERR-LOG-10.assumed: You probably expected a LEFT JOIN to keep every row of the left table, whatever WHERE says.
ERR-LOG-10.why: WHERE runs after the join. On a left row with no match, every column of the right table is missing, so a condition on a right-table column, such as `p.promo_type = 'clearance'`, is not true there and WHERE drops the row. The LEFT JOIN then works like an INNER JOIN.
ERR-LOG-10.model: Put a condition on the right table into the ON clause, as in `LEFT JOIN promotions p ON p.promo_id = ol.promo_id AND p.promo_type = 'clearance'`, so it decides which rows match without removing left rows. Keep WHERE for conditions on the left table, or for `IS NULL` when you want the rows with no match.

ERR-LOG-11.assumed: You probably expected the join type to change only the columns you get, not the rows.
ERR-LOG-11.why: An INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides, so a store with no orders or a product that never sold disappears. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and leaves the right side missing where nothing matches, and a FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the rows with no match from both sides. The wrong one drops rows the question wants, or keeps rows it does not.
ERR-LOG-11.model: Ask whether the question wants rows with no match. "Every store, including those with no orders" needs the stores on the left: `FROM stores s LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.store_id = s.store_id`. "Orders with their store" needs only matches, so an INNER JOIN. Then count the rows with no match to check.

ERR-LOG-12.assumed: You probably expected any two columns that look alike to make a good join.
ERR-LOG-12.why: A join pairs rows wherever the ON condition is true, whatever the columns mean. Joining `order_lines.product_id` to `promotions.promo_id`, or joining on a name instead of an ID, pairs rows that have nothing to do with each other, or none at all, and the numbers come out wrong with no error.
ERR-LOG-12.model: Join along a link the schema panel shows: a foreign key on one side and the primary key it points to on the other, such as `order_lines.order_id` to `orders.order_id`. When the key has two columns, as in `price_history`, match every column the question needs.

ERR-LOG-13.assumed: You probably expected SQL to read your conditions from left to right.
ERR-LOG-13.why: SQL applies AND before OR, the way multiplication comes before addition. So `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`, and the condition after AND applies to only one side of the OR.
ERR-LOG-13.model: Put brackets around the OR part whenever you mix AND and OR, for example `WHERE (country_code = 'BE' OR country_code = 'LU') AND store_type = 'outlet'`.

ERR-LOG-14.assumed: You probably expected the aggregate you chose to answer the question's wording.
ERR-LOG-14.why: Each aggregate answers a different question: SUM gives a total, AVG an average, COUNT how many, MIN the smallest and MAX the largest. A different one still returns a real number, just not the one asked for.
ERR-LOG-14.model: Translate the question's word into the function: 'total' is SUM, 'average' is AVG, 'how many' is COUNT, 'lowest', 'cheapest' or 'earliest' is MIN, and 'highest', 'most expensive' or 'latest' is MAX.

ERR-LOG-15.assumed: You probably expected `>` and `>=` (or `<` and `<=`) to keep the same rows.
ERR-LOG-15.why: They differ exactly at the boundary: `> 100` drops a row whose value is exactly 100, and `>= 100` keeps it. The question's wording decides which one is right.
ERR-LOG-15.model: 'At least' and 'or more' mean `>=`, 'more than' and 'over' mean `>`, 'at most' and 'or less' mean `<=`, and 'less than' and 'under' mean `<`. BETWEEN includes both of its ends.

ERR-LOG-16.assumed: You probably expected LIMIT to return the top rows on its own.
ERR-LOG-16.why: LIMIT only cuts the result after a number of rows. Without an ORDER BY in the right direction, those are whichever rows came first, and when values tie at the cut-off, only the tie-break the question states decides which row stays in.
ERR-LOG-16.model: Sort first, then cut: `ORDER BY` the ranking column with `DESC` for highest first or `ASC` for lowest first, add the question's tie-break as a second sort column, then `LIMIT n`.

ERR-LOG-17.assumed: You probably expected a missing value (NULL) to be handled the way the question says.
ERR-LOG-17.why: Arithmetic with a missing value gives a missing value, so `price * quantity` is missing when `quantity` is, and SUM, AVG and COUNT(col) skip it. If the question counts a missing value as 0 and you leave it as it is, those lines drop out and the average comes out too high; if it says to leave them out and you turn them into 0, the average is pulled down. `col IS NOT NULL` goes further: it removes the whole line, so its other columns stop counting too.
ERR-LOG-17.model: Read how the question treats missing values. If missing means 0, wrap the column in `COALESCE(col, 0)` before you calculate; if it says to ignore them, use the column as it is. Do not filter a line away for one missing value: each total already skips its own missing values, and the line still counts in the other totals.

ERR-LOG-18.assumed: You probably expected the rows to come out in the order the question asks for, either without an ORDER BY or with one on a different column or in the other direction.
ERR-LOG-18.why: SQL gives no guaranteed row order unless the query sorts the rows. Your rows are right, but when the question asks for an order, the order is part of the answer.
ERR-LOG-18.model: Add `ORDER BY` with the column the question names, `DESC` for highest or latest first and `ASC` for lowest or earliest first, and add the question's tie-break as a second sort column after a comma.

ERR-LOG-19.assumed: You probably expected rounding before you add up or divide to give the same answer as rounding at the end.
ERR-LOG-19.why: Each early rounding adds a small error, and SUM, AVG or a division adds those errors together, so the final number drifts a few cents or decimals away from the expected one.
ERR-LOG-19.model: Calculate with the full values and round once, around the final result: `ROUND(SUM(x), 2)`, not `SUM(ROUND(x, 2))`.

ERR-LOG-20.assumed: You probably expected the average of each row's ratio to equal the overall ratio.
ERR-LOG-20.why: AVG of a ratio gives every row the same weight, however big or small it is, so a line that sold 1 unit counts as much as a line that sold 1,000. The overall ratio weights each row by its size.
ERR-LOG-20.model: Add up the top and the bottom first, then divide once: `SUM(revenue) / SUM(units)` for an average selling price, not `AVG(revenue / units)`.

ERR-LOG-21.assumed: You probably expected a share and a percentage to be the same number.
ERR-LOG-21.why: A share of 0.15 and a percentage of 15 are the same amount on scales 100 times apart. Returning the share when the question asks for a percentage, or using a stored percentage such as `discount_pct` without dividing it by 100, puts every value off by a factor of 100.
ERR-LOG-21.model: Check the scale the question asks for. For a percentage, multiply the share by 100, as in `100.0 * part / whole`; to use a stored percentage in a calculation, divide it by 100 first, as in `discount_pct / 100.0`.

ERR-LOG-22.assumed: You probably expected LIKE to find the text whatever its letter case, or wherever it sits in the value.
ERR-LOG-22.why: LIKE is case-sensitive, so `'%pro%'` does not find Pro or PRO. A pattern also has to match the whole value: without a `%` on one side, the text must start or end right there, and each `_` stands for exactly one character.
ERR-LOG-22.model: Use ILIKE when the question says any letter case, and put a `%` wherever other text may come: `product_name ILIKE '%pro%'` finds pro anywhere in the name, in any case. Then check the pattern by hand against one value that should match and one that should not.

ERR-LOG-23.assumed: You probably expected your range to keep exactly the values the question describes.
ERR-LOG-23.why: BETWEEN low AND high keeps the values from low to high, both ends included, so `BETWEEN 20 AND 10` matches nothing at all. A range written with `>` or `<` leaves its end out and one written with `>=` or `<=` keeps it, so the wrong one drops or adds the rows that sit exactly on an end. For dates, each end is a whole day, so a wrong end moves a whole day in or out.
ERR-LOG-23.model: Put the low end first, as in `discount_pct BETWEEN 10 AND 20`. Then read the wording for each end: 'from ... to', 'at least' and 'up to' keep the end, while 'over', 'under', 'after' and 'before' leave it out. For a range of days, use `col >= first day AND col < day after the last day`, which cannot miss the last day.

ERR-LOG-24.assumed: You probably expected UNION to stack the two results exactly as they are.
ERR-LOG-24.why: UNION also removes duplicate rows across both parts and keeps one of each, so two order lines with the same values, or a product in both parts, count once. Counts and sums made from the result then come out too low.
ERR-LOG-24.model: Use UNION ALL to stack results and keep every row: `SELECT product_id FROM ... UNION ALL SELECT product_id FROM ...`. Use UNION only when the question asks for a list of different values, each once.

ERR-LOG-25.assumed: You probably expected a month or week number to stand for one period.
ERR-LOG-25.why: `month(order_ts)` gives 3 for March of every year, so grouping by it merges March 2024 with March 2025. A week number repeats in the same way, and ISO week 1 can start in late December: paired with the calendar year, 29 December 2025 lands in week 1 of 2025 instead of 2026. Truncating to another unit, such as the week where the question asks for the month, gives other periods than the question asks for.
ERR-LOG-25.model: Group by the start of each period with `date_trunc('month', order_ts)`, which keeps the year. For ISO weeks, use `date_trunc('week', order_ts)`, whose weeks start on Monday, or pair `isoyear(order_ts)` with `week(order_ts)`, never `year(...)` with a week number.

ERR-LOG-26.assumed: You probably expected `order_ts` to show Amsterdam time.
ERR-LOG-26.why: On the clean tables, every `_ts` column holds the moment in UTC, and on raw data each time is read as the task says. Where a column holds UTC, Amsterdam is 1 hour ahead in winter and 2 hours ahead in summer, so an order at 23:30 UTC is already the next day in Amsterdam. Taking the date, week or month straight from the column puts those late-evening orders on the day before.
ERR-LOG-26.model: Turn the UTC moment into Amsterdam time first, then take the date: `CAST(timezone('Europe/Amsterdam', timezone('UTC', order_ts)) AS DATE)`. A single `order_ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam'` is not enough: it reads the stored value as Amsterdam time and moves it the wrong way.

ERR-LOG-27.assumed: You probably expected the set operator you chose to keep the rows the question describes.
ERR-LOG-27.why: Each set operator answers a different question. UNION and UNION ALL stack both results, INTERSECT keeps only the rows in both, and EXCEPT keeps the rows of the first query that are missing from the second. EXCEPT also depends on the order: A EXCEPT B and B EXCEPT A give different rows, so writing the two queries the wrong way round answers the opposite question.
ERR-LOG-27.model: Say in words what you need, then pick the operator: 'in both' is INTERSECT, 'in either' is UNION, and 'in A but not in B' is `A EXCEPT B`, with A first. Then check one row you expect in the result and one you expect to be left out.

ERR-LOG-28.assumed: You probably expected a set operator to treat a missing value as `=` does, as never matching anything.
ERR-LOG-28.why: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT compare whole rows, and unlike `=` they count two missing values as the same. So when both queries return a row with a missing value, INTERSECT keeps one such row and EXCEPT removes it from the first query. A WHERE test or a join's ON never matches a missing value, so the same rows behave differently there.
ERR-LOG-28.model: Read whether the question counts rows with no value. When it leaves them out, filter them out in each query before the set operator, as in `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` in both parts. Then look for a row with a missing value in your result: keep it only when the question wants it.

ERR-LOG-29.assumed: You probably expected CASE to give each row the label of the branch that fits it best, whatever order the WHEN branches come in.
ERR-LOG-29.why: CASE tests its WHEN branches from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true. When an earlier test is wider, such as `units >= 2` before `units >= 5`, every row that passes the later test passes the earlier one too, so it takes the earlier label and the later branch never runs. Two rules that overlap work the same way: the one written first wins.
ERR-LOG-29.model: Order the branches so each row meets its own branch first: for bands, the highest cut-off first, as in `CASE WHEN units >= 5 THEN 'large' WHEN units >= 2 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'single' END`; for rules, the one that must win first, such as a test for a missing value. Then pick one row that passes two tests and check which label it gets.

ERR-LOG-30.assumed: You probably expected `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` to keep every row whose value is not in the subquery's list, even when that list holds a missing value.
ERR-LOG-30.why: `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and a comparison with a missing value is unknown, never true. So once the list holds one missing value, NOT IN returns no rows at all. `order_lines.promo_id` is missing on every line sold without a promotion, so `promo_id NOT IN (SELECT promo_id FROM order_lines)` finds no promotion, not even the ones never used.
ERR-LOG-30.model: Use NOT EXISTS, which only looks for a matching row and is not thrown by missing values: `SELECT p.promo_id FROM promotions p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_lines ol WHERE ol.promo_id = p.promo_id)`. Or keep NOT IN and leave the missing values out of the list: `NOT IN (SELECT promo_id FROM order_lines WHERE promo_id IS NOT NULL)`. Plain IN is safe: it keeps the rows that match.

ERR-LOG-31.assumed: You probably expected the subquery to compare each row with its own group, such as a product with the other products in its category.
ERR-LOG-31.why: A correlated subquery is worked out again for each outer row, and the link in its WHERE decides which rows it reads that time. Linked on the wrong column, such as the brand where the question compares by category, it reads another group, so each row is compared with the wrong group. Without the outer table's alias, `WHERE category_id = category_id` compares the inner table's column with itself, which is true on every row with a category, so each product is compared with every product.
ERR-LOG-31.model: Give the inner and the outer table different aliases, and link the inner table to the outer row on the column the question compares by: `SELECT p.product_id FROM products p WHERE p.unit_cost_eur > (SELECT AVG(p2.unit_cost_eur) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id)`. Then check one row by hand: what the subquery returns for it should be its own group's value.

ERR-LOG-32.assumed: You probably expected 'Audio', 'audio' and ' Audio ' to count as one value.
ERR-LOG-32.why: Text is compared character by character: a capital letter differs from a lower-case one, and a space at the start or end is a character too. So spellings of one key that differ only in letter case or spaces group into separate rows, and a join or a filter on them misses the rows written another way. `GROUP BY category_raw` gives one row per spelling, not one per category.
ERR-LOG-32.model: Clean the key the same way on both sides before you compare or group it: `GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(category_raw))`, or `ON LOWER(TRIM(a.sku)) = LOWER(TRIM(b.sku))`. Then count the different values before and after cleaning, and map any spelling that cleaning does not merge, such as a translated name, with CASE.

ERR-LOG-33.assumed: You probably expected text positions to start at 0, or the length in a substring to say where the cut ends.
ERR-LOG-33.why: SQL counts characters from 1, so `substr(sku, 1, 2)` gives the first 2 characters. The third number is how many characters to keep, not the position to stop at: `substr('VM-000123', 4, 6)` gives '000123'. A start or length one off cuts one character too many or too few, and DuckDB reads position 0 as the place before the first character, so `substr(sku, 0, 3)` gives only 2 characters.
ERR-LOG-33.model: Count the positions by hand on one value, starting at 1: in 'VM-000123' the digits start at position 4, so `substr(sku, 4)` keeps everything from there and `substr(sku, 4, 6)` keeps 6 characters. When the cut follows a separator rather than a fixed place, use `split_part(sku, '-', 2)`. Then check the result on the shortest and the longest values.

ERR-LOG-34.assumed: You probably expected `date_diff` to count whole days, months or years, and one date minus another to count every day from the first to the last.
ERR-LOG-34.why: `date_diff` counts the boundaries crossed between two moments, not whole periods: `date_diff('month', ...)` from 31 January to 1 February is 1, and from 1 January to 31 January is 0. On timestamps, `date_diff('day', ...)` from 23:00 to 01:00 the next morning is 1. And `end_date - start_date` counts the days between two dates, which leaves one end out: a promotion from 1 March to 31 March gives 30, though it ran on 31 days.
ERR-LOG-34.model: Read what the question counts. For the days between two dates, as in 'days from launch to first sale', subtract them: `first_sale_date - launch_date`. For the days a period lasts with both end days in, add 1: `end_date - start_date + 1`. Before you use `date_diff('month', ...)` or `date_diff('year', ...)` for whole periods, check it by hand on one pair of dates near a month end.

ERR-LOG-35.assumed: You probably expected a ratio with nothing to divide by, such as the average selling price of a product with no units sold, to count as 0.
ERR-LOG-35.why: When the denominator is 0 or missing, the ratio is unknown, not 0. `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` leaves it missing on purpose, and wrapping that in `COALESCE(..., 0)` turns it into a 0 that looks like a real result. An average of the ratio then counts those rows as zeros and comes out too low, and a list sorted by it puts them at the bottom as if they had done badly.
ERR-LOG-35.model: Keep the ratio missing where it cannot be worked out: `SUM(net_revenue_eur) / NULLIF(SUM(units), 0)`, with no COALESCE around it. If the question wants those rows counted, count them in a column of their own. Use 0 only when the question says a missing ratio counts as 0.

ERR-LOG-36.assumed: You probably expected each record to be in the table once.
ERR-LOG-36.why: Raw data can hold the same record twice, for example an order line sent again under a new `order_line_id`. COUNT(*) and SUM then count it twice, so totals come out too high and nothing warns you. `COUNT(DISTINCT order_line_id)` does not help when the copy has an ID of its own.
ERR-LOG-36.model: Check for copies before you report a total. Group by the columns that make two rows the same record, as the question defines it, not by the table's own ID: `SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_eur, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_eur HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`. Then count each record once, for example from `SELECT DISTINCT` over those columns in a CTE, and say how many copies you left out.

ERR-LOG-37.assumed: You probably expected a window function to work within each group, such as each store or each product, without naming the groups.
ERR-LOG-37.why: `OVER ()` and `OVER (ORDER BY ...)` treat the whole result as one window. With no PARTITION BY, a running total keeps adding across every store, a rank ranks all rows together, and a share divides by the grand total instead of the group's total.
ERR-LOG-37.model: Name the group in PARTITION BY, then the order inside it: on one row per store and day, `SUM(units) OVER (PARTITION BY store_code ORDER BY order_date)`. Then check two groups by hand: each starts again from its own first row, whose running total equals its own units.

ERR-LOG-38.assumed: You probably expected a window frame to hold the same rows whether it is written with ROWS, with RANGE or left out.
ERR-LOG-38.why: ROWS counts rows, while RANGE counts values of the ORDER BY column. With an ORDER BY and no frame, SQL uses RANGE from the first row to the current one, so rows that tie on the sort value share one running total instead of adding up one at a time. And `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is the last 7 rows, which covers more than 7 days when some days have no row.
ERR-LOG-38.model: Write the frame you mean. For a running total that adds one row at a time, give the ORDER BY a tie-break and use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. For the last 7 days, give every day a row first (a date spine) and use ROWS, or keep the gaps and use `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on a date column.

ERR-LOG-39.assumed: You probably expected a day, week or month with no rows to show up in your result with 0.
ERR-LOG-39.why: GROUP BY makes groups only from the rows that exist. A day with no orders has no row to group, so it does not appear at all rather than showing 0. A trend chart then skips the gap without a sign, and an average per day divides by too few days.
ERR-LOG-39.model: Start from a full list of periods, such as `calendar`, and LEFT JOIN the data to it, so every period keeps a row: `SELECT c.cal_date, COALESCE(SUM(s.units), 0) AS units FROM calendar c LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.order_date = c.cal_date WHERE c.cal_date >= '2025-03-01' AND c.cal_date < '2025-04-01' GROUP BY c.cal_date`. Filter the dates on the calendar side: a WHERE test on a column of `sales` would drop the days with no rows again.

ERR-CMP-01.assumed: You probably expected to need DISTINCT to stop the rows from repeating.
ERR-CMP-01.why: Your result is right, but DISTINCT changes nothing here: no two rows of the result can be the same, because each holds a value that is unique, such as `product_id`. DISTINCT still makes the engine compare every row, and where a join repeats rows, it hides that mistake instead of fixing it.
ERR-CMP-01.model: Before you add DISTINCT, ask whether two rows of the result could be the same. When each row holds a unique key, as in `SELECT product_id, product_name FROM products`, leave DISTINCT out; when a join repeats rows, fix the join instead.

ERR-CMP-02.assumed: You probably expected to need every table that sounds related to the question.
ERR-CMP-02.why: Your result is right, but one joined table adds no column and no filter the question needs. An extra join makes the query slower and harder to read, and on a 1:N link it can repeat rows when the query changes later.
ERR-CMP-02.model: Before you add a join, name the column or the filter it brings. When the table you start from already holds every column the question asks for, as `order_lines` holds `product_id`, leave the other table out.

ERR-CMP-03.assumed: You probably expected every condition in a grouped query to go in HAVING.
ERR-CMP-03.why: Your result is right, but this HAVING condition uses no aggregate, so it tests a value that is the same on every row of the group. WHERE can drop those rows before they are grouped, which is clearer and does less work.
ERR-CMP-03.model: Move a condition with no aggregate, such as `country_code = 'BE'`, to WHERE before GROUP BY, and keep HAVING for conditions on a group's totals, such as `COUNT(*) > 10`.

ERR-OUT-01.assumed: You probably expected the answer to count as right with an extra column, a missing column or a differently named column.
ERR-OUT-01.why: The output contract asks for {expected_columns} column(s) with the names it lists, and your query returned {actual_columns}. The columns are part of the answer: an extra one changes what each row means, and a missing one leaves part of the question unanswered.
ERR-OUT-01.model: Select exactly the columns in the output contract, in its order, and use AS to give each one the name it lists. A missing comma also turns the next column name into an alias, as in `SELECT city country_code`, so check the commas in your SELECT list.

ERR-OUT-02.assumed: You probably expected a value to count as right whatever its type, for example the text '10' for the number 10, a date written as text, or a whole number written with decimals, such as 2.0 for 2.
ERR-OUT-02.why: SQL keeps text, numbers and dates as different types: the text '10' never equals the number 10, and the engine stops when it cannot turn one type into another. Each column must have the type the output contract shows, in the place it shows it. In screen mode, as in an online SQL test, whole numbers and numbers with decimals are different types too: a count that comes back as 2.0, after `* 1.0` or a CAST to a decimal, does not match the whole number 2.
ERR-OUT-02.model: Return each column in the contract's type and order: leave numbers and dates unformatted rather than casting them to text, and compare text columns with quoted text such as `'BE'` and number columns with plain numbers such as `10`. Return a count as a whole number: use `* 1.0` or a CAST to a decimal only on a value that has decimals, such as a rate.
